plot_extraction.response_text:
At a summer cottage, carefree Julie Marvis lingers in the only bathtub while her more conservative sister, Lois, impatiently waits to bathe before meeting Mr. Calkins, a divorced literary man her mother dislikes. After discovering that Julie entered without clothes, a robe, or even a towel, Lois indignantly leaves and takes the towel with her.

Mr. Calkins then appears outside the bathroom window. Unable to see inside, he mistakes Julie for Lois, while Julie mischievously allows the error to continue. They banter about clothing, literature, and love as Julie invents explanations for the sounds of bathwater. Calkins finally declares his love, just as the real Lois returns. Horrified to find him speaking to her naked sister, Lois faints. Calkins announces that he is coming inside to help her, while Julie grabs Lois’s dropped towel and prepares to escape the bathtub.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written as a one-act farce in dramatic script form, combining theatrical stage directions with an unusually intrusive, conversational narrator. Its governing tone is urbane, playful, irreverent, and knowingly artificial. Rather than concealing the mechanics of drama, the narration foregrounds them: it comments on the set, anticipates the audience’s suspicions, identifies mistaken identity as the “old rusty pivot” of the plot, and openly manipulates suspense. The result is a metatheatrical style in which the narrator, characters, and imagined audience all seem complicit in the joke.

The opening uses detailed visual description but immediately turns description into comedy. The repeated fisherman-and-ship frieze is presented with mock fascination, while the bathtub is personified through automotive imagery, as though it were an outdated racing car with a “high tonneau” and short legs. Objects are not rendered naturalistically so much as converted into comic personalities. The room’s sparse arrangement has the precision of stage design: every physical feature, especially the bathtub, window, door, towel, taps, and water pipes, is positioned to enable later misunderstandings. Apparently decorative details often conceal practical theatrical functions, although the narrator jokingly insists that the frieze is “not in the plot.”

The narration speaks directly to the audience in a breezy first-person plural or second-person manner: “we deduce,” “you begin to suspect,” and “you’ve guessed it.” This produces the voice of a witty master of ceremonies rather than an invisible storyteller. It continually breaks the dramatic illusion with asides about theatrical convention, audience reaction, casting resemblance, and plot construction. Hyperbolic references to gasps, applause, and murmurs turn the fictional spectators into participants. The final phrase, “A Belasco midnight,” similarly treats stage lighting as both a technical effect and a cultural joke, closing the piece with conspicuous theatricality rather than realism.

Dialogue supplies most of the momentum. Exchanges are short, quick, and combative, with one line frequently overturning the assumptions of the last. Julie’s speech is the stylistic centre: spontaneous, slangy, associative, and driven by non sequiturs, puns, comic analogies, mock solemnity, and deliberate literalism. She converts “Godliness” and “Cleanliness” into nicknames, parodies fairy-tale narration, plays with euphemisms such as “au naturel,” and answers practical objections with absurd fantasy. Her jokes often depend on switching registers without warning—from childish games to faux-philosophical pronouncements, from colloquial irritation to ornate storytelling. Lois’s comparatively direct, censorious language acts as a straight-man counterweight. The young man’s sentimental and literary rhetoric provides a second target, allowing Julie to puncture pretension through misquotation, confused attribution, bath-related digressions, and slang.

The diction mixes early twentieth-century American colloquialism with elevated or foreign expressions. Phrases such as “golly,” “darn,” “kid you,” “low-brow,” “jumping cats,” and “fella” coexist with “ablutions,” “surpassing loveliness,” “au naturel,” and mock-classical allusions. This collision of registers is a major source of humor. Contemporary references to popular entertainers, fashionable dances, automobiles, telephones, literary celebrities, and theatrical producers give the piece a distinctly Jazz Age or post–World War I social texture. Some references are intentionally garbled by Julie, making cultural sophistication itself part of the farce.

The sentence style differs sharply between stage directions and dialogue. Descriptive passages favor long, accumulating sentences with parenthetical interruptions, em dashes, comic qualifications, and delayed punch lines. Dialogue is more clipped and rhythmically agile, often using fragments, repetitions, contractions, and interruptions. Parenthetical performance cues—“sweetly,” “desperately,” “sentimentally,” “after some consideration”—shape timing and frequently create irony by contrasting a character’s manner with the content of the line. Repetition is used as a comic mechanism, particularly when confusion escalates or a speaker attempts to preserve a false assumption.

The humor relies on dramatic irony, mistaken identity, sexual innuendo, euphemism, and controlled concealment. The audience knows Julie is naked in the bathtub and knows that the young man mistakes her for Lois; the young man knows neither. Almost every innocent remark therefore acquires a double meaning. Questions about what Julie is “wearing,” whether she will “come out,” and why water can be heard all operate on two levels. The erotic element remains teasing rather than explicit, sustained through strategic visibility: only Julie’s head, throat, shoulders, and arms are seen, while the audience’s curiosity is repeatedly acknowledged and exploited. Her nudity becomes both a plot device and an expression of her refusal to be embarrassed.

Characterization is broad but efficient. Julie is mischievous, self-possessed, imaginative, anti-authoritarian, and verbally dominant. Her apparent naivety is paired with sharp social insight, especially when she mocks experience, literary vanity, and amateur character analysis. Lois represents decorum, convention, and anxious respectability, though sibling rivalry keeps her from becoming merely prudish. Mr. Calkins is a recognizable comic type: the self-important literary man whose cultivated speech masks vanity and romantic conventionality. Character emerges primarily through verbal rhythm and response rather than introspection.

Structurally, the piece follows a compact farcical escalation. It begins with the private inconvenience of a missing towel, introduces the risk of discovery, brings the mistaken suitor to a window from which he cannot see the bathtub, and sustains the misunderstanding through increasingly implausible explanations. The water pipes, soap splash, goldfish excuse, and Lois’s entrance function as precisely timed comic beats. The climax occurs when visual recognition finally destroys the false identity, after which the threat of the young man entering forces an immediate blackout. The ending withholds the anticipated exposure and converts it into a final audience-directed tease.

Thematically, the story lightly opposes youthful spontaneity to social convention, bodily ease to prudery, and irreverent intelligence to cultivated pretension. It does not pursue these conflicts seriously; they remain materials for comedy. Its signature style is therefore best described as metatheatrical drawing-room farce: visually economical, dialogue-heavy, sexually suggestive without explicitness, rich in period slang and topical allusion, and organized around rapid repartee, comic misrecognition, and an amused awareness of its own theatrical machinery.

generation.response_text:
## CLEANLINESS, WITH COMPLICATIONS  
*A One-Act Farce*

**THE PERSONS**

**JULIE MARVIS**, who has never mistaken embarrassment for a virtue.  
**LOIS MARVIS**, her sister, who has.  
**MR. ADRIAN CALKINS**, a literary gentleman, divorced, serious, and thirty-seven in a favorable light.  
**THE AUDIENCE**, unwilling accomplices.

---

The bathroom at the Marvis summer cottage is large enough to encourage hope and inconvenient enough to punish it.

Across the walls marches a blue frieze of fishermen drawing blue nets from a blue sea while, immediately behind them, a blue ship sails with calm determination toward what appears to be the bathroom door. The fishermen have been hauling the same three fish since 1906. They are not in the plot. We mention this firmly because experienced audiences, observing any repeated design in a first act, expect it to conceal either a secret passage or the deceased uncle’s will.

At the left is a door leading to the hall. At the right, rather high in the wall, is a broad window opening upon a veranda roof. A person outside may see the upper portion of a person standing within, but not the lower portion; and a person reclining in the bathtub may see somebody at the window while remaining almost entirely unseen. Nature did not arrange this window. A dramatist did.

The bathtub occupies the centre of the room with the aggressive dignity of an elderly touring car. It has a high porcelain tonneau, four short clawed legs, and taps suggesting the brass goggles of a motorist who has taken a wrong turn and intends never to admit it. Beside it stands a chair. On the chair there is nothing.

This nothing is important.

At the rise, **JULIE MARVIS** is in the tub. Only her head, throat, bare shoulders, and one speculative knee—withdrawn before anyone can become statistical—are visible. Her dark hair is piled recklessly on top of her head and secured with a yellow pencil. She is twenty-two, which is an age at which a pencil may be considered a hair ornament and consequences a form of entertainment.

She is sailing a cake of soap along the rim.

**JULIE**  
(in a deep nautical voice)  
Iceberg to starboard! Women and authors first!

The soap slips into the water.

**JULIE**  
There goes American literature.

A pounding comes at the door.

**LOIS**  
Julie!

**JULIE**  
No forwarding address.

**LOIS**  
You’ve been in there forty minutes.

**JULIE**  
Thirty-eight. The other two were ablutions.

**LOIS**  
Open this door.

**JULIE**  
I’m not dressed for callers.

**LOIS**  
You’re never dressed for anything on time.

**JULIE**  
That’s what makes getting dressed worth watching.

The knob turns uselessly.

**LOIS**  
Mother says I’m to have the bathroom immediately.

**JULIE**  
Tell Mother Cleanliness refuses to surrender to Godliness.

**LOIS**  
I don’t know what you mean.

**JULIE**  
You’re Godliness. I’m Cleanliness. We were separated in childhood by a cruel grammarian.

**LOIS**  
Mr. Calkins will be here at four.

**JULIE**  
Then he can be Next-to-Godliness.

**LOIS**  
Julie!

**JULIE**  
I don’t see why a literary man needs you scrubbed. Aren’t they supposed to admire the natural woman—barefoot in the wheat, with a soul like a sunset and no knowledge of punctuation?

**LOIS**  
Adrian does not admire vulgarity.

**JULIE**  
That must make shaving difficult.

There is a brief silence outside, the sort in which a sister counts ten and discovers she has counted the same murder ten times.

**LOIS**  
I laid out your things on the bed.

**JULIE**  
Sweet of you.

**LOIS**  
Did you bring a robe in there?

**JULIE**  
No.

**LOIS**  
Your slippers?

**JULIE**  
No.

**LOIS**  
Your clothes?

**JULIE**  
Lois, if I had brought my clothes into the bathtub they’d be damp. Even I know that.

The door flies open. **LOIS** enters because Julie, with the splendid inconsistency of the carefree, has locked nothing. Lois is twenty-eight, fair, composed, and dressed in a pale summer frock which looks as if it has never sat down impulsively. Over one arm she carries a fresh towel.

She stops.

**LOIS**  
You haven’t anything with you!

**JULIE**  
I have soap, water, and a philosophy.

**LOIS**  
You came through the hall without a stitch?

**JULIE**  
Not exactly. I wore an expression.

**LOIS**  
Suppose someone had seen you?

**JULIE**  
Then it would have been someone’s lucky Thursday.

**LOIS**  
Mother is downstairs!

**JULIE**  
Mother never looks up before breakfast. It’s one of her moral principles.

**LOIS**  
It’s nearly four.

**JULIE**  
Then she never looks up before tea.

Lois places the towel on the chair, then notices that this is precisely what Julie wants.

**LOIS**  
You did this deliberately.

**JULIE**  
I never do anything deliberately. It spoils the surprise.

**LOIS**  
You knew I had an appointment.

**JULIE**  
A rendezvous.

**LOIS**  
An appointment.

**JULIE**  
With a divorced man on a summer afternoon? Darling, if you call that an appointment, what do you call the dentist?

**LOIS**  
Mr. Calkins’s marriage was a tragedy.

**JULIE**  
Most marriages are, if you write reviews of them afterward.

**LOIS**  
You’ve met him twice.

**JULIE**  
That’s enough to dislike a person intelligently. Love takes three meetings because one has to forget the first two.

**LOIS**  
Mother has prejudiced you.

**JULIE**  
Mother says he’s conceited, gloomy, and writes books in which married people stare at rain. I made up my own mind to agree with her.

**LOIS**  
Adrian understands women.

**JULIE**  
Has he apologized?

**LOIS**  
He has suffered.

**JULIE**  
Everybody has suffered. I had mumps during the fox-trot craze, but I don’t publish novels about my neck.

Lois snatches up the towel.

**JULIE**  
Here! Put that back.

**LOIS**  
No.

**JULIE**  
That towel is my future.

**LOIS**  
You may remain where you are until I have bathed and dressed.

**JULIE**  
You can’t bathe while I’m here.

**LOIS**  
Then perhaps you’ll learn foresight.

**JULIE**  
I tried foresight once. Everything I foresaw was dull.

**LOIS**  
You can call for Mother.

**JULIE**  
I’d sooner send a wireless to Siam.

**LOIS**  
Good.

**JULIE**  
Lois, if you take that towel, history will hold you responsible.

**LOIS**  
History may telephone me.

She exits, taking the towel. The door closes.

Julie regards it.

**JULIE**  
Lady Macbeth with Turkish cotton.

She sinks lower in the tub. We now possess the essential elements of high comedy: one naked young woman, one absent towel, and a door. Sophocles required a royal house and several generations of sin, but Sophocles did not understand summer rentals.

A man’s face appears at the window.

This is **MR. ADRIAN CALKINS**. He wears white flannels, a soft collar, and the expression of a person arriving unexpectedly but not, he hopes, undesirably. His hair is brushed backward in a manner which must be renewed after every strong opinion. He carries a book.

Julie sees him. He cannot see the tub, concealed from his angle by the high porcelain side. He sees only Julie’s head and shoulders above it, which might belong to a young woman sitting in a low chair. You begin to suspect the old rusty pivot upon which our plot will revolve. Do not groan. It has supported better plays than this.

**CALKINS**  
Lois!

Julie opens her mouth, closes it, and considers virtue. Virtue loses.

**JULIE**  
Good afternoon.

**CALKINS**  
I startled you.

**JULIE**  
You startled several of me.

**CALKINS**  
I came over the veranda roof. Your mother was in the garden.

**JULIE**  
So you chose the alpine route.

**CALKINS**  
She still objects to me.

**JULIE**  
Mother objects to almost everything that can vote.

**CALKINS**  
I couldn’t endure the formalities today.

**JULIE**  
Were they chasing you?

**CALKINS**  
May I come in?

Julie’s eyes travel from the window to the door, from the door to the vacant chair, and from the vacant chair to heaven, which has plainly withdrawn its management.

**JULIE**  
No!

**CALKINS**  
No?

**JULIE**  
I mean—you’re charming where you are. Like a portrait with ivy.

**CALKINS**  
You’re alone?

**JULIE**  
Profoundly.

**CALKINS**  
Then why shouldn’t I enter?

**JULIE**  
Because I’m not receiving.

**CALKINS**  
You seem dressed.

**JULIE**  
Appearances have started wars.

**CALKINS**  
What are you wearing?

**JULIE**  
My hair.

**CALKINS**  
(charmed)  
Your humor is different today.

**JULIE**  
It shrank in the wash.

A tiny slosh is heard as she moves.

**CALKINS**  
What was that?

**JULIE**  
A goldfish.

**CALKINS**  
You keep goldfish in your room?

**JULIE**  
Only one. He’s sensitive and can’t stand bowls. They make him feel watched.

**CALKINS**  
This isn’t your room.

**JULIE**  
He travels.

Calkins smiles with literary tolerance—the smile of a man willing to let reality be fanciful if he can take credit for noticing.

**CALKINS**  
You’ve been avoiding me, Lois.

**JULIE**  
Have I been successful?

**CALKINS**  
Cruelly.

**JULIE**  
Then why criticize technique?

**CALKINS**  
Your letters became guarded.

**JULIE**  
There are burglars everywhere.

**CALKINS**  
Yesterday, when I spoke of my new book, you changed the subject.

**JULIE**  
What did I change it to?

**CALKINS**  
Tennis.

**JULIE**  
A better seller.

**CALKINS**  
You said my heroine needed exercise.

**JULIE**  
Did she?

**CALKINS**  
She was dying of disillusionment.

**JULIE**  
Then exercise would have tired her into believing something.

**CALKINS**  
You liked Helena when I first described her.

**JULIE**  
I hadn’t lived with her for three hundred pages.

**CALKINS**  
You haven’t read the manuscript.

**JULIE**  
That may be why I still like her.

He leans upon the window ledge, wounded but fascinated.

**CALKINS**  
I had not suspected this lightness in you.

**JULIE**  
It’s the hot water. It brings out hidden colors.

**CALKINS**  
Hot water?

A pipe gives a long metallic knock beneath the tub.

**JULIE**  
The goldfish has a hammer.

**CALKINS**  
Lois—

**JULIE**  
He’s building a little garage.

**CALKINS**  
There’s something strange here.

**JULIE**  
There generally is when one looks closely at plumbing.

**CALKINS**  
I can hear water.

**JULIE**  
The sea.

**CALKINS**  
We’re half a mile from the sea.

**JULIE**  
Sound travels. That’s why gossip beats automobiles.

Calkins shifts position. Julie promptly sinks until only her eyes and hair are visible.

**CALKINS**  
Where did you go?

**JULIE**  
South.

**CALKINS**  
Please sit up.

**JULIE**  
I’m looking for a motive.

**CALKINS**  
For what?

**JULIE**  
Your coming through a bathroom window.

**CALKINS**  
I came because I must speak to you before your mother poisons your feeling against me.

**JULIE**  
Mother never poisons. She serves prejudice cold with mayonnaise.

**CALKINS**  
She considers me dangerous because I have been married.

**JULIE**  
Experience always frightens people who haven’t enjoyed it.

**CALKINS**  
You don’t condemn me, then?

**JULIE**  
I don’t know enough about you. Condemnation without research is low-brow.

**CALKINS**  
You know my past.

**JULIE**  
Only the parts with good punctuation.

**CALKINS**  
I told you everything.

**JULIE**  
Nobody ever tells everything. Half the human race would stop speaking if that were the rule.

He becomes solemn. Julie recognizes the approach of a speech and searches discreetly for the soap, perhaps as a weapon.

**CALKINS**  
My marriage taught me that love without spiritual companionship is merely a room in which two strangers hear each other breathe.

**JULIE**  
Couldn’t they open a window?

**CALKINS**  
You make a joke of pain.

**JULIE**  
Pain makes such poor conversation by itself.

**CALKINS**  
Clara never understood my need to create.

**JULIE**  
Did you create at breakfast?

**CALKINS**  
Sometimes.

**JULIE**  
Then I understand Clara.

**CALKINS**  
She mocked my ideals.

**JULIE**  
Ideals look funny in pajamas.

**CALKINS**  
Lois, this is not like you.

**JULIE**  
That’s the most encouraging thing you’ve said.

A footstep sounds in the hall. Julie freezes. The audience freezes, too, though it has paid to do so in comfort.

The knob turns. The door is locked now—not by foresight but because Lois, departing in wrath, turned the key from outside and pocketed it. This is either a fortunate accident or shameless construction. We prefer “construction.”

**LOIS’S VOICE**  
Julie?

Julie raises one warning finger toward Calkins.

**CALKINS**  
(whispering)  
Who is that?

**JULIE**  
Julie.

**CALKINS**  
Your sister?

**JULIE**  
Frequently.

**LOIS’S VOICE**  
Are you still in there?

**JULIE**  
Where else would I be?

**LOIS’S VOICE**  
Mother wants the blue powder.

**JULIE**  
Tell her I’m using it.

**LOIS’S VOICE**  
For what?

**JULIE**  
The goldfish has a rash.

There is a silence.

**LOIS’S VOICE**  
You’re an idiot.

**JULIE**  
Family resemblance!

Lois’s footsteps retreat.

Calkins studies Julie with new tenderness.

**CALKINS**  
You didn’t tell her I was here.

**JULIE**  
She’s nervous about wildlife.

**CALKINS**  
You protected me.

**JULIE**  
Don’t sentimentalize it. I protected the window.

**CALKINS**  
I had thought your sister understood me.

**JULIE**  
Julie understands everybody. That’s why she doesn’t approve of them.

**CALKINS**  
She dislikes me.

**JULIE**  
She thinks you’re an old man.

**CALKINS**  
I’m thirty-seven!

**JULIE**  
To twenty-two, thirty-seven is an historic monument with visiting hours.

**CALKINS**  
She is impertinent.

**JULIE**  
She’s young.

**CALKINS**  
Youth is no excuse for shallowness.

**JULIE**  
What is youth an excuse for? It ought to excuse something. Otherwise it’s just bad skin and no money.

Calkins is silent, struck despite himself.

**CALKINS**  
That’s rather good.

**JULIE**  
Write it down and misquote me.

**CALKINS**  
You’ve changed since yesterday.

**JULIE**  
Perhaps yesterday was badly cast.

**CALKINS**  
You seem freer—more vivid.

**JULIE**  
I’m au naturel.

**CALKINS**  
In manner?

**JULIE**  
Among other departments.

He fails to understand. We do not. A murmur travels through the imaginary orchestra seats and is suppressed by ushers of unusual moral stamina.

**CALKINS**  
I used to feel a reserve in you.

**JULIE**  
I’ve mislaid nearly everything today.

**CALKINS**  
Your reserve, your formality—

**JULIE**  
My towel.

**CALKINS**  
What?

**JULIE**  
My—towel of ivory. A poem. By—Shelley Longfellow.

**CALKINS**  
There is no such poem.

**JULIE**  
It was suppressed in Boston.

She reaches for the soap, misses, and splashes water over the side.

**CALKINS**  
There! Water again.

**JULIE**  
The goldfish applauded.

**CALKINS**  
I’m coming in.

**JULIE**  
Adrian, if you put one literary knee over that sill, I’ll scream the roof loose.

**CALKINS**  
You called me Adrian.

**JULIE**  
I called you several things internally.

**CALKINS**  
You never called me Adrian before.

**JULIE**  
Perhaps intimacy is a disease. It advances with the temperature.

He gazes at her. His expression softens into the dangerous earnestness of a man who has mistaken bewilderment for revelation.

**CALKINS**  
Do you know what has happened?

**JULIE**  
Yes, and when Lois finds out, it will happen harder.

**CALKINS**  
For months I’ve admired your serenity, your delicacy, your grave understanding. But today—today I see the woman beneath them.

Julie glances down into the tub.

**JULIE**  
You have remarkable eyesight.

**CALKINS**  
The real woman: capricious, mocking, elemental.

**JULIE**  
Don’t forget damp.

**CALKINS**  
I love this new courage in you.

**JULIE**  
It’s easy to be courageous when there’s nowhere to run.

**CALKINS**  
You have ceased to fear life.

**JULIE**  
I’m beginning to fear the hallway.

**CALKINS**  
Lois, listen to me.

**JULIE**  
I’ve been trying not to.

**CALKINS**  
My first marriage failed because we built upon illusion. I will make no such mistake again. Between us there must be absolute candor.

**JULIE**  
Let’s begin tomorrow.

**CALKINS**  
Now.

**JULIE**  
Tomorrow has better facilities.

**CALKINS**  
Tell me what you feel.

**JULIE**  
Warm around the edges.

**CALKINS**  
You evade me because you are moved.

**JULIE**  
That is not why I’m avoiding movement.

**CALKINS**  
Can’t you come nearer the window?

**JULIE**  
Not without launching the tub.

**CALKINS**  
Then let me see your face.

She rises a cautious inch. A gleaming bare shoulder appears. Calkins sighs.

**CALKINS**  
Surpassing loveliness!

**JULIE**  
Jumping cats.

**CALKINS**  
You’re like Botticelli’s Venus.

**JULIE**  
She had attendants with towels.

**CALKINS**  
You’ve read Botticelli?

**JULIE**  
Not since I left school.

**CALKINS**  
He was a painter.

**JULIE**  
Then he should have used shorter sentences.

Calkins laughs, genuinely this time.

**CALKINS**  
You destroy all my poses.

**JULIE**  
I thought they were furniture.

**CALKINS**  
That is what I need! Someone who will laugh me out of solemnity, challenge me, keep me young—

**JULIE**  
At thirty-seven you need a nurse with roller skates.

**CALKINS**  
Someone precisely like you.

Julie’s mischief pauses. For the first time she looks faintly alarmed—not by him, perhaps, but by the speed with which a joke can acquire a hat, coat, and legal intentions.

**JULIE**  
Now don’t go making anything permanent. This is only Thursday.

**CALKINS**  
Why did I never see it before?

**JULIE**  
Bad lighting.

**CALKINS**  
I thought love would come with music, with some great spiritual recognition.

**JULIE**  
It generally trips over the plumbing.

The pipe bangs again with orchestral emphasis.

**CALKINS**  
Even that seems like a sign.

**JULIE**  
It’s a sign the cottage needs repairing.

He presses both hands to the sill.

**CALKINS**  
Lois, I love you.

At this precise moment the key turns in the door.

We could delay it. We could permit Julie an answer, or send a bird through the window, or cause the blue fishermen to drop their net. But farce, like an express train and a jealous sister, has a schedule.

The door opens. **LOIS** enters with the towel over her arm.

**LOIS**  
Julie, Mother says if you don’t—

She sees Calkins at the window.

He turns and sees Lois.

He looks at Lois. He looks at Julie. He looks again at Lois, because hope is a persistent little animal.

**CALKINS**  
Lois?

**LOIS**  
Adrian!

**JULIE**  
Introductions seem unnecessary.

**LOIS**  
What are you doing here?

**CALKINS**  
I was speaking to—you.

**LOIS**  
To me?

**JULIE**  
Spiritually.

**CALKINS**  
But she— You— There are two—

**JULIE**  
That’s what Mother says when expenses come in.

Lois advances and, following Calkins’s horrified stare, sees the bare shoulders above the bathtub, the wet arm, the high porcelain rim, and at last the whole magnificent geometry of the misunderstanding.

**LOIS**  
You have been talking to my sister!

**CALKINS**  
I thought she was you.

**JULIE**  
He has a gift for character analysis.

**LOIS**

# The Cartographer of Lost Roads

Every morning, before the bells of Saint Orra struck six, Elias Vale walked to the eastern gate of Bellweather and drew the road that had vanished during the night.

Sometimes it was a narrow lane between two houses. Sometimes it was a stone stairway leading down to the river. Once, in the coldest week of winter, an entire avenue disappeared, taking with it twelve shops, three gardens, and a fountain shaped like a sleeping lion.

The people returned. The buildings returned. Even the lion returned, its stone mouth still stained green by water. But the road connecting them to the rest of the city was gone.

Without a road, no one could reach those places.

They remained visible in the distance, like islands across an uncrossable sea. A baker might stand at the door of his shop and wave, while his customers shouted from a square only twenty yards away. Yet if either tried to cross the empty space where the street had been, they found themselves walking back to where they had started.

That was why Bellweather needed a cartographer.

Elias carried a black leather case containing paper, compasses, rulers, ink, and a brass instrument his mother had called a pathfinder. It resembled a pocket watch with seven hands, none of which told the time. When held over a lost road, the hands trembled toward whatever fragments of memory remained.

He would kneel, place his paper against the ground, and begin.

A road was never merely stone and soil. It was footsteps, destinations, and decisions. To restore one, Elias had to draw not only its shape but its purpose. He marked where children had raced hoops, where lovers had paused beneath balconies, where funeral carts had turned toward the cemetery. When the map was complete, he signed his name in the lower corner.

Then the road returned.

The stones rose first, pushing through the pale emptiness. Gutters appeared, followed by lampposts, doorsteps, and the shadows of trees. The stranded citizens applauded, and Elias folded the map into the city archive, where thousands of restored roads slept in drawers.

For eleven years, his hand never failed.

Then, one rainy morning, the road to his own house disappeared.

Elias knew before he reached the corner. His pathfinder began to shake inside its case, the brass hands rattling like trapped insects. He hurried through the market, past merchants raising striped awnings against the rain, and stopped beside a boarded watchmaker’s shop.

Across a narrow expanse of gray nothingness stood his home.

It was a modest house with blue shutters and a copper roof. Smoke curled from the chimney. In the upstairs window, behind glass webbed with rain, stood his daughter, Mira.

She was fourteen and small for her age, with dark hair she cut herself and a serious face that often made adults feel they had said something foolish. When she saw Elias, she lifted one hand.

He waved back.

Mira opened the window.

“Father?”

“I’m here.”

“The front door won’t open onto anything.”

“Don’t try to leave.”

“I already did.”

Elias gripped his case. “Are you hurt?”

“No. I stepped through and came back into the kitchen.”

This was common around vanished roads. Doors and paths folded inward. A person could walk from a bedroom into the same bedroom, or climb a staircase for hours only to arrive at its first step.

“Stay inside,” he called. “I’ll restore it.”

He set his paper on a crate beneath the watchmaker’s awning. He had mapped Larkspur Lane many times during routine surveys. He knew its length, its width, and the number of stones between his doorstep and the corner. He knew the old chestnut tree leaned six degrees south. He knew rain collected beside the drain because Mira had lost a red boot there when she was five.

Elias began to draw.

The pathfinder’s seven hands spun.

He sketched the first line. It faded.

He tried again, pressing harder. The ink vanished before it dried.

Across the emptiness, Mira watched from the window.

Hours passed. The rain thickened. A crowd gathered and then slowly dispersed as people returned to their work. By noon, Elias had ruined twenty-three sheets of paper.

At last, Master Renn came from the archive.

Renn had trained Elias in the art of cartography when Elias was still young enough to believe maps existed only to tell travelers where they were. Now Renn was nearly eighty. His back had bent, but his eyes remained bright and unforgiving.

He stood beside Elias and studied the missing lane.

“How long?” he asked.

“Since before six.”

“And the ink?”

“Won’t hold.”

Renn lifted the pathfinder. Its hands blurred.

“I have seen this once before,” he said.

Elias turned. “Where?”

“The north quarter, forty-two years ago. A footbridge vanished. The cartographer could not restore it because someone had taken away its destination.”

“The destination is there.” Elias pointed toward his house.

“The building is there. That is not always the same thing.”

At the window, Mira held up a slate. She had written:

WHAT IS WRONG?

Elias forced a smile and raised one finger, asking her to wait.

“What happened to the bridge?” he asked quietly.

“It was forgotten.”

“By whom?”

“By everyone who had loved what waited on the other side.”

Elias stared at his house.

His wife, Clara, had chosen its blue shutters. She had planted lavender beneath the windows and painted tiny stars on Mira’s bedroom ceiling. After Clara died, Elias stopped tending the lavender, and it turned woody and wild. He rarely looked at the stars.

But he had not forgotten.

“I love my daughter,” he said.

“I do not doubt it.”

“Then the house has a destination.”

“Does it?”

The question struck him as cruel.

Renn returned the pathfinder. “A map can measure distance, Elias. It cannot create a reason to cross it.”

Then he left.

By evening, Mira lit the lamps inside the house. Their warm glow seemed impossibly far away.

Elias sat beneath the awning, surrounded by spoiled pages. He drew the lane from memory. He drew it from city records. He drew it as it had looked in spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Each attempt dissolved.

At midnight, Mira appeared again.

“You should sleep,” he called.

“So should you.”

“I’m working.”

“You’re staring at the paper.”

“That is part of the work.”

“It’s the part you’re best at.”

Despite himself, he laughed.

Mira smiled, but it faded quickly. “Will I be here long?”

“No.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I will find a way.”

She looked over her shoulder into the empty rooms behind her. “There’s enough food for a week.”

“You won’t need it.”

“And the water still runs. Although it tastes like Tuesday.”

“What does Tuesday taste like?”

“Disappointing soup.”

“That sounds accurate.”

She rested her arms on the windowsill. “Father, when did we last eat together?”

“Yesterday.”

“You read survey reports through supper.”

“We were at the same table.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Elias looked down at the blank paper.

A bell sounded somewhere in the city, marking one in the morning.

Mira closed the window.

The following day, Elias went to the archive.

It occupied the old royal palace, though no monarch had ruled Bellweather for two centuries. Maps covered every wall. Maps hung from rafters. Maps lay in oak cabinets that filled halls once used for feasts and dancing.

Elias searched the records for Larkspur Lane.

He found the first survey, drawn eighty-seven years ago. He found plans for the sewers, gas lines, and chestnut trees. He found every repair and alteration, including the replacement of a cracked curb outside number seven.

None of the documents could restore the road.

Near dusk, Renn found him asleep over a map.

“You are searching in the wrong place,” the old man said.

“This is where the maps are.”

“No. This is where the paper is.”

Elias sat up. “If you know something, tell me.”

“I told you. Find the destination.”

“My daughter is the destination.”

“Then map your daughter.”

Elias frowned. “A person cannot be mapped.”

“Everything that can be lost can be mapped.”

Renn walked away before Elias could demand an explanation.

Elias returned to the missing lane carrying an armful of fresh paper. Mira had placed a chair at the upstairs window and was reading by lamplight.

He sat beneath the awning and wrote her name in the center of a page.

Mira Vale.

The ink remained.

Around it he drew a circle and began adding what he knew.

Fourteen years old.

Born during the bell storm.

Dark hair. Gray eyes.

Likes honey cake.

Dislikes thunder.

Good at arithmetic.

He paused.

Was she still afraid of thunder? He remembered her crawling into his bed during storms, but that had been years ago. Perhaps she had outgrown it.

He crossed out dislikes thunder.

The ink vanished from the entire sheet.

He tried again.

This time he drew Mira at seven, missing her two front teeth. Then at nine, running beside the river. Then at eleven, holding the wooden bird she had carved for him.

The drawings were accurate, but none felt alive.

He realized he was mapping memories of someone who no longer existed.

At sunrise, Mira opened the window and found him surrounded by sketches.

“Is that supposed to be me?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“My head isn’t shaped like a turnip.”

“It is an early draft.”

“And I haven’t worn braids since I was ten.”

“I know.”

“You drew braids.”

“I can see that.”

She leaned farther out. “Why are you drawing me?”

“Master Renn said I must map the destination.”

“I’m the destination?”

“Yes.”

Her expression became uncertain. “You could have just asked.”

“Asked what?”

“Where I am.”

“I know where you are.”

“No,” she said. “You know where the house is.”

She closed the window.

Elias stared at the imperfect portraits until the meaning of her words settled over him.

He packed his case.

At the archive, he requested leave from his duties. Then he visited Mira’s school.

Her teacher, Mistress Pell, seemed surprised to see him.

“Is Mira unwell?” she asked.

“In a manner of speaking.”

He looked at the rows of desks. Mira’s was near the back, beside a window. The wood was covered with tiny carved feathers.

“Why feathers?” he asked.

Mistress Pell blinked. “Because she likes birds.”

“She does?”

“She spends every midday break on the roof, watching them. She can identify thirty-seven species by flight alone.”

Elias thought of the wooden bird on his desk. He had used it as a paperweight for three years.

“Is she a good student?”

“In some subjects.”

“Arithmetic?”

“Terrible.”

Elias stared at her.

“Mira says numbers behave like prisoners,” Mistress Pell continued. “She feels sorry for them and lets them escape.”

“Then what is she good at?”

“History. Music. Drawing. Asking questions no one wants to answer.”

From the school, Elias went to the bakery.

The baker knew Mira. So did the fishmonger, the lamplighter, two bridge keepers, and an old woman who fed pigeons beside the courthouse. Mira carried bread to the old woman each Thursday. She helped the lamplighter clean soot from the glass. She had persuaded the bridge keepers to let her build a nesting box beneath the western arch.

Elias had known none of this.

At the river, he found a girl named Tessa repairing a red kite.

“You’re Mira’s father,” she said.

“Yes. You are her friend?”

“Best friend.”

Elias waited, embarrassed that he had never heard her name.

Tessa tightened the kite string between her fingers. “Mira says you fix roads.”

“I restore them.”

“She says you fix everyone else’s road so you don’t have to travel your own.”

Children, Elias thought, should not be allowed to speak like ancient judges.

“What does she mean?”

Tessa shrugged. “Ask her.”

That evening, Elias stood at the edge of the blank space and called up to the window.

Mira appeared, holding a candle.

“I visited your school,” he said.

“Why?”

“To map you.”

“That sounds unpleasant.”

“You like birds.”

“You discovered my dark secret.”

“You are not good at arithmetic.”

“I never claimed to be.”

“You take bread to a woman named Mrs. Arno. You built a nesting box beneath West Bridge. Your best friend is Tessa Quill, and you have been teaching the lamplighter to read.”

Mira was silent.

“I should have known,” Elias said.

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

She looked toward the rooftops. A flock of starlings crossed the evening sky, folding and unfolding like dark cloth.

“After Mother died,” Mira said, “you stopped asking questions.”

“I thought questions upset you.”

“No. Answers upset you.”

Elias felt the truth of it.

Clara’s death had not been sudden. For a year, their home had filled with medicines, whispered conversations, and the bitter smell of boiled herbs. Mira had asked whether her mother would recover. Elias had said yes. She had asked whether he was afraid. Elias had said no. She had asked whether he would stay with her after the funeral. He had promised he would.

Instead, he had returned to work the following morning.

Roads were easier than grief. A road could be measured. A road could be restored by following rules. There were no rules for entering a silent house where a dead woman’s shoes remained beneath the bed.

“I didn’t know how to come home,” he said.

Mira’s face softened, though only a little. “You live there.”

“I know.”

“No,” she replied. “You sleep there.”

The candle flickered between them.

“What should I have done?” Elias asked.

“You could have missed her with me.”

Mira closed the window.

Elias remained at the vanished lane until the stars appeared.

Then he placed a clean sheet on the crate.

He did not draw the road.

He drew a girl sitting on a rooftop beneath a wide sky. Around her wheeled birds of every kind: swifts with narrow wings, silver gulls, black rooks, red-breasted finches. He drew her hands stained with ink and bread flour. He drew a red kite caught in a chimney. He drew carved feathers across a school desk and a nesting box beneath a bridge.

But the pathfinder remained restless.

The map showed who Mira was in the city. It did not show where she was to him.

Elias took another page.

For a long time, he could not make the first mark.

Then he drew a small room in winter. Clara lay sleeping in bed, exhausted from illness. On the floor, six-year-old Mira had arranged blankets over three chairs, making a tent. Elias remembered lying beneath it while Mira explained that the world outside had frozen solid and they were the last explorers alive.

He drew Mira at the funeral, her hand reaching for his while he spoke to the undertaker.

He drew the breakfast table the next morning, with one chair empty and Mira watching him put on his coat.

He drew every supper at which he had hidden behind papers.

He drew all the times she had waited at a window.

The ink held.

Near dawn, he reached the bottom of the page. There was no room left for a road.

Mira opened the window.

“Father,” she called, “the house is changing.”

Behind her, the wallpaper had begun to fade. The blue shutters lost their color. Tiles slipped soundlessly from the roof and vanished before they struck the ground.

The destination was disappearing.

Elias seized another sheet. His hands shook so badly that the compass rolled into the gutter.

He could not map the past quickly enough to save her.

So he drew the future.

He drew two figures carrying chairs onto a rooftop to watch birds. He drew himself burning survey reports in the fireplace while Mira laughed. He drew them eating supper at a table with no papers on it. He drew a journey to the sea, which Mira had never seen. He drew Clara’s birthday, not as a day of silence, but as a day when they would cook her terrible onion stew and tell stories about her.

Last, he drew a doorway.

On one side stood Mira. On the other stood Elias.

Between them was no road, no stone, no measured distance—only a single step each had to choose to take.

The seven hands of the pathfinder stopped.

For one terrible moment, nothing happened.

Then the blank space cracked.

A stone appeared beneath Elias’s left foot. Another rose before it. Across the gap, the doorstep of his house returned, shining with rain. The chestnut tree unfolded from the air, branches first, then trunk, then roots. Gutters, lamps, and garden walls emerged in a rush.

Larkspur Lane came back with the sound of a thousand people sighing.

Elias ran.

The front door opened before he reached it. Mira stood there in her nightclothes, her face pale from a week of poor sleep.

He stopped on the threshold.

For years, he had imagined that returning home required confidence, answers, and the right words.

It did not.

It required only that he enter.

“I miss her,” he said.

Mira’s eyes filled.

“So do I.”

He stepped inside, and she wrapped her arms around him.

They stood in the hall while rain tapped the copper roof and the restored city woke around them.

Later that morning, Elias cooked breakfast. He burned the eggs, undercooked the bread, and dropped an entire jar of plum preserve on the floor.

Mira ate everything except the broken glass.

At noon, they carried two chairs onto the roof.

She taught him the difference between a rook and a crow. He repeatedly confused them, and she repeatedly corrected him. Then a peregrine falcon crossed the sky, too fast for Elias to see clearly.

“Did you catch it?” Mira asked.

“No.”

“You have to look where it’s going, not where it was.”

He glanced at her. “That sounds like something Master Renn would say.”

“Then he sounds very wise.”

“He is unbearable.”

They sat until evening.

In the weeks that followed, roads continued to vanish from Bellweather. Elias still rose before dawn and carried his black leather case through the city. But he no longer believed that roads were made from stone, or that destinations were merely places.

When a lane disappeared, he spoke to the people who had walked it. He asked what waited at the end, what had happened along the way, and why anyone would wish to cross it again.

His maps changed.

They became crowded with faces, promises, quarrels, songs, market smells, childhood games, and names written in margins. The archive complained that his work was becoming untidy. Master Renn only smiled.

Years later, when Elias retired, Mira inherited the black case.

By then, she had become the city’s youngest master cartographer and its first to map the skies. She charted the paths of swallows and storms, the yearly turning of geese, and the invisible roads birds followed across oceans.

On her first morning as keeper of Bellweather’s roads, she found Elias waiting by the eastern gate.

“You don’t work here anymore,” she told him.

“I thought you might need help.”

“I don’t.”

“Good.”

He gave her the brass pathfinder. Its seven hands rested quietly beneath the glass.

Mira slipped it into her coat.

“Will you be home for supper?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“I’m making onion stew.”

She groaned. “Mother’s recipe?”

“I found it in the blue cupboard.”

“She was a terrible cook.”

“She truly was.”

Mira kissed his cheek and walked into the waking city.

Elias watched until she turned the corner.

Then he went home—not because a map directed him there, nor because the stones remembered his feet, but because there was a table to set, a story to tell, and someone he loved already traveling toward him.
